theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Who is a customer?
options: Only a person who pays in cash at the front counter
Only a large company that signs a contract
Only someone who has made a complaint
Anyone who receives a product or service from you

questions.stem: In a workshop, who is an internal customer?
options: A person who comes in to buy a new gate from the business
A co-worker who needs your work to do their job
A supplier who delivers steel to the yard
A tourist who stops to ask for directions

questions.stem: Why are first impressions important in customer service?
options: Customers often decide quickly whether to trust you
They are the only thing a customer remembers
They mean you can skip listening to what the customer wants
They decide how much the customer must pay

questions.stem: Marlon is going to a customer's home in Ocho Rios to look at a job. Which is the best way for him to present himself?
options: In his oldest clothes, because the job may be dirty
In any clothes, as long as he brings his tools
Clean work clothes or uniform, with his ID badge
Dressed up in his best going-out clothes and jewellery

questions.stem: A customer walks into the workshop office. What should you do first?
options: Greet them politely and ask how you can help
Finish your phone call, then look up at them
Wait for them to speak before you say anything
Point them to the boss's office without speaking

questions.stem: You are busy serving one customer when another one arrives. What should you do?
options: Leave the first customer and serve the new one
Ignore the new customer until you are finished
Tell the new customer to come back another day instead
Smile, greet them and say you will be with them soon

questions.stem: What is active listening?
options: Waiting for the customer to stop so you can talk
Writing down everything while looking at the page
Giving full attention and checking you understood
Nodding at everything the customer says to you

questions.stem: Which of these is an open question?
options: Is the gate for the front of the house?
What would you like the gate to look like?
Do you want it painted black?
Is Tuesday a good day for us to come?

questions.stem: When is a closed question (one with a yes or no answer) most useful?
options: When you want the customer to tell you a lot
When you first meet the customer
When you want to hear the customer's ideas
When you need to confirm one detail

questions.stem: After a customer explains what they need, what should you do?
options: Start the work straight away
Tell them about your last job
Repeat the main points back to check
Ask them to write it all down for you

questions.stem: Which body language shows a customer that you are interested in what they say?
options: Arms folded and looking at your phone
Facing them, eye contact and a nod
Turning away to look at your work
Leaning on the wall with hands in pockets

questions.stem: Which is the best way to speak to a customer who does not work in the trade?
options: Use plain words and explain any trade terms
Use lots of trade words to sound expert
Speak very fast so that you save their time
Speak loudly so they know you are sure

questions.stem: A customer says, "My lights keep going off." What is the best first step?
options: Tell them they need a whole new wiring system
Say it is probably the power company's fault
Ask questions to find out when and where it happens
Sell them a set of new light bulbs straight away

questions.stem: A customer wants a cheap gate, but also needs it to keep out intruders. What should you do?
options: Sell them the cheapest gate and say nothing
Refuse the job because the budget is too low
Sell the dearest gate so that they are safe
Explain the options and help them choose

questions.stem: How should you answer the business phone?
options: Say "Yes?" and wait for the caller to talk
Greet the caller, give the business and your name
Say "Hello" and pass the phone to someone else
Let it ring out so that the caller leaves a message

questions.stem: You take a phone message for your supervisor. What must the message include?
options: The caller's name, number, the message and the time
Only the caller's first name and the fact that they called
Your opinion of how the caller sounded
The time you plan to pass the message on

questions.stem: A customer asks when their gate will be ready. You are not sure. What should you say?
options: "Tomorrow", so that they are happy for now
"I don't know, that's not my job"
"Whenever the welder gets round to it"
"I will check and call you back by 3 p.m."

questions.stem: Why is it important to do what you said you would do, when you said you would?
options: So that you can charge the customer more
So that the customer can trust you and the business
So that you can finish work early each day
So that the customer does not ask you any more questions

questions.stem: An elderly customer has trouble hearing you. What should you do?
options: Shout every word as loudly as you can
Talk to the person with them instead
Face them, speak clearly and check they understood
Write everything down and hand it over without speaking

questions.stem: A customer in a wheelchair comes to the office counter, which is high. What is the best action?
options: Come round the counter to talk at their level
Talk to them over the counter as normal
Ask them to send someone else next time
Speak to the person pushing the wheelchair

questions.stem: A visitor from overseas does not understand some of the local words you use. What should you do?
options: Keep talking the same way; they will pick it up
Speak more slowly and use simple standard English
Laugh about it and change the subject
Ask them to go and find someone to translate

questions.stem: How should you treat customers of different backgrounds, ages and beliefs?
options: Treat older customers better than young ones
Give the best service to customers who look rich
Treat them how you think people like them want
Treat every customer with the same respect

questions.stem: You are doing electrical work in a customer's home. How should you protect their property?
options: Lay dust sheets and move furniture with permission
Move anything that is in your way without asking
Leave the cleaning to the customer when you finish
Work fast and fix any damage later on

questions.stem: At the end of a job at a customer's house, what should you do?
options: Leave quickly so that the customer does not ask questions
Leave the offcuts so that the customer can use them
Clean up, explain the work and check they are happy
Ask the customer to sweep up the dust

questions.stem: You are welding a gate on site in a customer's yard and children are watching. What should you do?
options: Let them watch closely so that they learn the trade
Carry on and tell them not to stare at the light
Put up screens and ask an adult to keep them away
Give them spare goggles and let them watch

questions.stem: The power to a customer's house must be switched off while you work on the wiring. What should you tell the customer first?
options: When the power will be off and when it will be back
Nothing, because they do not need to know
To switch it back on themselves if they need to use something
To phone the power company to complain

questions.stem: Why should a complaint be welcomed?
options: It means the customer will pay more next time
It proves the worker made a mistake on purpose
It lets you blame the supplier for the problem
It shows what to fix and helps keep the customer

questions.stem: A customer complains that their new gate scrapes the ground. What should you do first?
options: Explain that the ground is not level, so it is not your fault
Listen to the whole complaint without interrupting
Tell them the welder will call them some time
Offer them their money back straight away

questions.stem: Which order is best for handling a complaint?
options: Listen, apologise, solve the problem, thank and follow up
Explain your side, argue the point, then listen to them
Apologise, blame the supplier, listen, then solve the problem
Solve the problem, listen, then send the bill

questions.stem: A customer starts shouting at you about a delay. What should you do?
options: Shout back so that they know you will not be pushed around
Walk away and leave them in the office alone
Stay calm, listen, and speak in a quiet, steady voice
Tell them they are wrong and explain why

questions.stem: A customer becomes threatening and you feel unsafe. What should you do?
options: Stay and argue until the customer calms down
Threaten them back so that they will stop
Pretend nothing is happening and carry on
Move to a safe place and get your supervisor

questions.stem: A customer asks for a big discount that you are not allowed to give. What should you say?
options: "Yes, and I will sort it out with my boss later"
"I can't approve that, but I will ask my supervisor"
"No, and there is nothing more to talk about"
"Maybe, if you pay me in cash today"

questions.stem: Why should you know your business's rules on refunds, warranties and repairs?
options: So that you can change them for each customer
So that you give customers correct and fair answers
So that you never have to ask your supervisor anything at all
So that you can refuse every complaint

questions.stem: What is a good way to find out if customers are happy with your service?
options: Guess from how much they paid
Wait until someone complains
Ask other workers what they think
Ask for feedback after the job

questions.stem: A week after fitting a security light for Mrs Brown in Spanish Town, Odane calls her to check that it is working well. Why is this good service?
options: It lets him charge her for an extra visit
It means he can skip testing the work
It shows care and finds any problem early
It is the only way to get paid for the job

questions.stem: Why should customer details and job notes be recorded accurately?
options: So the next person can give the right service
So you can sell the customer list to other companies
So the files look full when the boss checks
So the customer can be charged twice

questions.stem: A neighbour asks you what work you did inside a customer's house and what it cost. What should you do?
options: Tell them, because it is good advertising
Tell them about the work but not the price
Show them a photo of the customer's invoice on your phone
Politely say you cannot share a customer's details

questions.stem: Which is an example of going the extra mile for a customer?
options: Charging more for a faster job without asking
Doing the job as asked and nothing more
Pointing out a loose hinge and offering to fix it
Doing extra work and adding it to the bill later

questions.stem: You realise you gave a customer the wrong collection date. What should you do?
options: Contact them quickly, apologise and give the right date
Say nothing and hope they come on the right day
Blame the office for the mistake when they call
Quietly change the date in the job book so nobody finds out

questions.stem: How does good teamwork help customer service?
options: Each worker can blame the others for mistakes
Information is passed on and jobs are done on time
Fewer people need to talk to the customer at all
Workers can take longer breaks during the day

questions.stem: A customer sends a message to the business phone asking about a price. When should you reply?
options: As soon as you can, in working hours
Only when you have time at the weekend
Never, because prices must be given in person
After a week, so they think you are busy

questions.stem: How should you write a message to a customer by phone or email?
options: In capital letters so that it stands out
With slang and emojis so that it is friendly
Politely, clearly and with correct spelling
As short as possible, with no greeting at all

questions.stem: A customer asks an electrician to remove the RCD (the safety trip switch) because it keeps tripping. What should he do?
options: Remove it, because the customer is always right
Explain why it is needed and offer to find the fault
Remove it, but tell the customer to be very careful from now on
Leave without saying anything to the customer

questions.stem: Before starting a job, why should you agree the work, the price and the finish date with the customer?
options: So that you can change them later without telling them
So that the job takes longer and costs more
So that the customer cannot ask any questions
So that you both know what to expect

questions.stem: Which attitude gives the best customer service?
options: Polite, helpful and honest
Fast, loud and in a hurry
Quiet, distant and formal
Friendly but careless with details

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Workers often wear an ID badge when they visit customers. What does ID stand for?
What is the name for a written promise that faulty work or parts will be put right free of charge for a set time?
What do we call communication without words, such as facial expressions, posture and gestures?
What do we call a customer who comes back to the business again and again?
What is the word for keeping a customer's private information secret?
What is the name of the document that gives the customer a fixed price for the work before the job is agreed?
What is the name of the document sent to a customer asking them to pay for work that has been done?
What do we call the written list of the level of service a business promises to give every customer?
A message to a customer says "ETA 2 p.m." What does ETA stand for?
What is the small printed card with your name, the business name and a phone number that you give to customers?
What do we call the date or time by which you have promised to finish a job?
What two-word term means how pleased customers are with the service they received?
What is the recorded message called that a caller leaves on a phone when nobody answers?
What word means trade or technical words that most customers will not understand?
Where should a business record every complaint and what was done about it?

essays.stem: Explain what quality customer service means in a welding or electrical business, and why it matters to the business.
essays.modelAnswer: Quality customer service means giving every customer a polite, honest and reliable service that meets their needs, from the first phone call to the follow-up after the job. It means listening carefully to what the customer wants, giving clear advice and fair prices, doing safe and neat work on time, keeping the customer informed, cleaning up and dealing well with any problem. For example, a welder who fits a gate on the agreed day, explains how to look after it and checks that it closes well is giving quality service. So is an electrician who protects the floor, explains the power cut times and tests the work. It matters because happy customers come back, pay on time and tell their friends and family, so the business gets more work. Poor service loses customers and gives the business a bad name.
markingPoints: Polite, honest, reliable service that meets the customer's needs
Listening, clear advice, fair prices, safe and neat work on time
Keeping the customer informed, cleaning up and handling problems
Gives a suitable trade example
Matters because of repeat work, word of mouth and the business's good name

essays.stem: Describe how you would find out exactly what a customer needs when they come to the workshop asking about a job.
essays.modelAnswer: I greet the customer politely, give my name and ask how I can help. I let them explain in their own words and listen carefully without interrupting, keeping eye contact and nodding. Then I ask open questions to learn more, such as "What will the grill be used for?" or "Which rooms need extra sockets?" I ask closed questions to confirm details, such as sizes, colours, the address and the date they need it by. I ask about their budget and explain the choices in plain words, so that they can decide. I write the details on a job request form, and then repeat the main points back to check that I have understood. If a site visit is needed to measure, I agree a date and time. Finally I tell them what will happen next and when they will hear from us.
markingPoints: Greets politely and lets the customer explain
Listens actively without interrupting
Uses open questions to explore and closed questions to confirm
Discusses budget and options in plain words; records the details
Repeats back to check, and agrees the next step

essays.stem: Explain how listening, questioning and body language help you communicate well with customers.
essays.modelAnswer: Good listening means giving the customer my full attention, not interrupting, and checking that I have understood by repeating the main points. It shows respect and makes sure I do the right job. Questioning helps me get the information I need. Open questions, such as "How do you use the back door?", get the customer talking, while closed questions, such as "Is it 900 mm wide?", confirm a detail. Body language is what my face, hands and posture show. Facing the customer, making eye contact, nodding and having a relaxed, open posture show that I am interested and can be trusted. Folded arms, looking at my phone or turning away show that I do not care, even if my words are polite. When listening, questioning and body language work together, the customer feels valued and I understand exactly what they need.
markingPoints: Listening: full attention, no interrupting, checking understanding
Open questions to get information, with an example
Closed questions to confirm details, with an example
Positive body language: facing, eye contact, nodding, open posture
Negative body language spoils polite words; together they make the customer feel valued

essays.stem: Describe how to deal professionally with a customer's phone call, and how to take an accurate message.
essays.modelAnswer: I answer the phone quickly and greet the caller, giving the business name and my own name, and asking how I can help. I speak clearly and politely, and I smile, because it can be heard in the voice. I listen carefully and write notes as the caller speaks. If I can answer the question I do so; if not, I do not guess. If the person they want is not there, I offer to take a message. I write down the caller's name and how to spell it, their phone number, what the message is about, how urgent it is, and the date and time of the call. I read the message and the number back to check them. I tell the caller who will call back and roughly when, and thank them for calling. Then I pass the message on quickly and check that it has been dealt with.
markingPoints: Answers promptly with a greeting, business name and own name
Speaks clearly and politely, listens and makes notes; does not guess
Message includes name, number, subject, urgency, date and time
Reads the details back to check them
Says when someone will call back, thanks the caller and passes the message on quickly

essays.stem: Describe how you should behave and work when you are doing a job in a customer's home or business.
essays.modelAnswer: I arrive on time in clean work clothes with my ID, introduce myself and explain what I will do and how long it will take. I ask where I can park, where I can work and where I can put my tools, and I ask permission before moving furniture. I protect floors and furniture with dust sheets. I tell the customer about anything that will affect them, such as the power or water being off, noise, or fumes from welding or painting. I keep the work area safe, with screens and barriers to keep children and pets away, and I never leave tools or cables where someone could trip. I am polite, do not smoke, play loud music or use the customer's things without asking, and I keep private matters private. At the end I clean up fully, explain the work and how to look after it, and check that the customer is happy.
markingPoints: Arrives on time, well presented, introduces self and explains the work
Asks permission and protects the customer's property
Tells the customer about power cuts, noise or fumes
Keeps the area safe for the family, children and pets
Polite and respectful of privacy; cleans up, explains and checks satisfaction

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you would handle a customer who complains that a job was not done properly.
essays.modelAnswer: First I listen to the whole complaint without interrupting, keeping calm and showing that I am taking it seriously. I write down the details. Then I apologise that they have had a problem, even before I know the cause, and thank them for telling us. I ask questions to understand exactly what is wrong, and if I can, I look at the work, for example the gate that scrapes or the light that will not switch on. I explain what I can do within the business's rules, such as returning to adjust the gate or test the circuit, and agree a time with the customer. If the problem is outside what I am allowed to decide, I pass it to my supervisor and tell the customer when they will hear back. I record the complaint and the action taken. After the problem is fixed, I follow up to check that the customer is now happy.
markingPoints: Listens fully, stays calm and records the details
Apologises and thanks the customer
Finds out exactly what is wrong
Agrees a solution within their authority, or refers to the supervisor
Records the complaint and follows up to check the customer is satisfied

essays.stem: Explain how you would deal with a customer who is angry or upset, and what you would do if you felt unsafe.
essays.modelAnswer: I stay calm and do not take it personally, because the customer is usually angry about the problem, not about me. I let them speak and listen without interrupting or arguing. I keep my voice low and steady and my body language open, and I keep a safe distance. I show that I understand, for example "I can see why you are upset that the gate is late". Once they are calmer, I ask questions to find the facts and explain what I can do, and when. I do not make promises that I cannot keep. If I cannot solve the problem, I bring in my supervisor. If the customer becomes threatening or violent, my safety comes first: I do not argue back, I move away to a safe place, get help from my supervisor or co-workers and, if needed, call the police. Afterwards I report and record what happened.
markingPoints: Stays calm and does not take it personally
Listens without arguing; low, steady voice and open body language
Shows understanding and offers what can be done, without false promises
Brings in the supervisor if the problem cannot be solved
If unsafe, moves away, gets help or calls the police, then reports the incident

essays.stem: Explain how you would give good service to customers with different needs, such as an elderly person, a person with a disability, or a visitor who speaks another language.
essays.modelAnswer: Every customer should be treated with the same respect, but the way I help may change. With an elderly customer I am patient, speak clearly and face them so they can see my lips, and I give them time to decide. I may write down the main points, such as the price and the date, so that they can check them later. With a person with a disability, I speak to them directly, not to the person with them, and I ask how I can help rather than guessing. For a wheelchair user I come round the counter to talk at their level and make sure the way in is clear. With a visitor who speaks another language, I speak slowly, use simple words, avoid slang and jargon, and use drawings, photos or a translation app on a phone if needed. In every case I check that the customer has understood.
markingPoints: Same respect for every customer, with help adjusted to their needs
Elderly: patience, clear speech, time, written key points
Disability: speaks to the person directly, asks how to help, physical access
Other language: slow, simple words, no slang, pictures or a translation app
Checks the customer has understood

essays.stem: Explain why following up with customers and collecting their feedback are important, and describe how you would do it.
essays.modelAnswer: Following up shows the customer that the business cares after the job is paid for. It can find a small problem early, such as a gate that needs a hinge adjusted or a light sensor that is set wrongly, before it becomes a complaint. Feedback tells the business what it does well and what it needs to improve, so that service gets better over time. Happy customers who are asked for feedback are also more likely to recommend the business. To do it, I call or message the customer a few days after the job, at a suitable time, and politely ask whether everything is working well and whether they were happy with the service. I may ask them to fill in a short feedback form. I write down what they say, thank them, deal with any problem quickly and pass the feedback to my supervisor.
markingPoints: Shows care and builds trust
Finds problems early, before they become complaints
Feedback shows what to improve and brings recommendations
Calls or messages at a suitable time, or uses a short form
Records the feedback, thanks the customer, acts on problems and passes it on

essays.stem: Explain how working within the business's rules and passing on information to your team helps to give quality customer service.
essays.modelAnswer: The business has rules on prices, discounts, refunds, warranties, safety and the time to reply to customers. When every worker follows the same rules, customers get fair and correct answers, and nobody is promised something the business cannot give. If a customer asks for something outside my authority, such as a big discount, I pass it to my supervisor instead of guessing. Passing on information is just as important. If I take a message, learn that a customer has changed the size of a grill, or find out that materials will be late, I tell the right person quickly and write it on the job sheet. Then the welder, the electrician or the office can act on it, and the customer does not have to repeat themselves. Good teamwork means jobs are done right the first time and on time, which keeps customers happy.
markingPoints: Follows the business rules so that customers get fair, correct answers
Refers matters outside their authority to the supervisor
Passes on messages and changes quickly to the right person
Records information on job sheets so that the team can act
Teamwork gets jobs done right and on time

practical1.title: Role play: welcome a customer, find out their needs and record a job request
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a set of customer cards, for example a home owner who wants a steel gate and window grills, a shop owner who wants extra sockets and an outside light, and a villa manager who wants a broken steel handrail repaired. Set up a simple counter or office area. Take turns so that every member plays the service worker once and the customer once, while the others watch and fill in an observation sheet. The service worker greets the customer, listens, asks open and closed questions, explains choices in plain words, fills in the job request form, reads the details back to check them, and agrees the next step, such as a site visit date. After each role play, the group gives short feedback to the service worker. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical, with the completed forms and observation sheets. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A table and chairs set up as a counter or office
Pens, a clipboard and a calendar for booking visits
A phone or tablet for photos (with everyone's permission)
photos: The counter or office area set up, with forms ready
A member greeting the customer at the start of a role play
A member asking questions and writing on the job request form
The member reading the details back to the customer
A completed job request form for each member
The group giving feedback, with the observation sheets
checklist: Greeted the customer politely and gave their name
Used positive body language: facing the customer, eye contact, open posture
Listened without interrupting and asked suitable open and closed questions
Explained choices in plain words, without jargon
Filled in the job request form fully, clearly and correctly
Read the details back to check them and agreed the next step
Played the customer role fairly and filled in the observation sheet for others
safety: Keep the role-play area tidy, with chairs and bags out of the walkway
Use only made-up customer names, addresses and phone numbers
Take photos only with the permission of everyone in them
Stop the role play if anyone feels upset or uncomfortable, and tell the assessor

practical2.title: Role play: handle a customer complaint and follow it up
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a set of complaint cards, for example a gate that scrapes the ground, lights that keep tripping off, a job finished two days late, or dust and offcuts left behind in a customer's home. Take turns so that every member handles one complaint as the service worker while another member plays the customer and the rest observe. The service worker listens, apologises, asks questions to find the facts, offers a solution within the business's rules or passes it to the supervisor, and fills in the complaint record. Then each member makes a short follow-up call (role play) a few days later and records the outcome. Together, make a one-page poster showing your group's steps for handling a complaint. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical, with the complaint records and the poster. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Chart paper and markers for the poster
A table and chairs set up as a counter or office
A phone or tablet for photos (with everyone's permission)
photos: A member listening to the customer at the start of a complaint
The member writing on the complaint record while asking questions
The member explaining the solution or the next step
The finished poster of the complaint steps
checklist: Listened to the whole complaint calmly, without interrupting or arguing
Apologised and thanked the customer for telling them
Asked questions to find the facts
Offered a fair solution within the rules, or passed it to the supervisor correctly
Did not make promises that could not be kept
Filled in the complaint record clearly, with the action and the date
Made the follow-up call politely and recorded the outcome
Helped to make the group poster
safety: Role plays must stay calm: no shouting at each other and no physical contact
Take photos only with the permission of everyone in them
Stop the role play if anyone feels upset, and tell the assessor
